tips.title: Motor effect out, generator effect in
tips.body: The **motor effect** puts a **current in** and gets **movement out**. The **generator effect** puts **movement in** and gets a **potential difference out**. They are the same physics run in opposite directions — a motor and a generator are the same device.

tips.title: Fleming's left hand is for motors
tips.body: **Left hand** for the **motor** effect. **First finger = Field**, **seCond finger = Current**, **thuMb = Motion**. Hold the three at right angles. The letters do the remembering: F, C, M in order down the hand.

tips.title: F = BIl is given; V = IR is not
tips.body: **$F = BIl$ is on the AQA physics equation sheet**, and so are the transformer equations. $V = IR$ and the power equations are **not** — they must be recalled. Knowing which is which saves memorising the wrong things.

tips.title: Transformers need alternating current
tips.body: A transformer works because a **changing** magnetic field induces a pd in the secondary coil. A **steady dc** current gives a **steady** field, which induces **nothing**. This is why the National Grid uses **ac**.

tips.title: Alternator gives ac, dynamo gives dc
tips.body: An **alternator** generates **ac**; a **dynamo** generates **dc**. The letters line up — **a**lternator to **a**c, **d**ynamo to **d**c — and the difference is in how the coil connects to the circuit.

steps.title: Electromagnetism
steps.body:
**When a current flows through a conducting wire a magnetic field is produced around the wire.** This is where the whole topic starts.

**The strength of that field depends on two things**: the **current** through the wire, and the **distance** from the wire. More current gives a stronger field; further away gives a weaker one.

**The field around a straight wire** is a series of **concentric circles** around it, getting further apart as you move away — which is the field getting weaker.

**Shaping a wire to form a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field** created by the current. A solenoid is a coil of wire, and coiling it means the field from each turn **adds** to the field from the others.

**Inside a solenoid the magnetic field is strong and uniform** — the same strength and direction throughout. **Outside**, the field **has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet**, with what behaves like a north pole at one end and a south at the other.

**Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid**, because iron is easily magnetised and its own magnetism adds to the field.

**An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core.** Its great advantage over a permanent magnet is that it can be **switched off**, and its strength **varied** by changing the current.

steps.title: The motor effect
steps.body:
**When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.**

Notice the wording: the force acts on **each other**. The wire is pushed, and the magnet is pushed back just as hard.

**Fleming's left-hand rule** gives the directions. Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the **left** hand at **right angles** to each other:

- **First finger — Field**, pointing from north to south
- **seCond finger — Current**, in the conventional direction
- **thuMb — Motion**, the direction of the force

**Left hand for the motor effect.** The capital letters in **F**ield, se**C**ond and **M**otion run in order down the hand, which is the easiest way to keep it straight.

**The size of the force** is given by:

$$F = B I l$$

where **B** is the **magnetic flux density** in **tesla (T)**, **I** the current in amperes and **l** the length in metres. This applies **for a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field**.

**This equation is given on the physics equation sheet** — you apply it rather than recall it. That is worth knowing, because $V = IR$ and the power equations are **not** given.

**A worked value:** a wire of length 0.3 m carrying 2 A at right angles to a field of 0.5 T feels a force of $0.5 \times 2 \times 0.3 = $ **0.3 N**.

steps.title: Motors and loudspeakers
steps.body:
**A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate. This is the basis of an electric motor.**

**Why it rotates.** The coil has two sides carrying current in **opposite** directions — one side going away from you, the other coming back. Fleming's left-hand rule therefore gives forces in **opposite** directions on the two sides: one is pushed **up** and the other **down**. A pair of opposite forces on opposite sides of an axle makes the coil **turn**.

**Keeping it turning.** Once the coil reaches the vertical, the forces would start to turn it back. A **split-ring commutator** reverses the current direction every half turn, so the force on each side reverses at exactly the right moment and the coil keeps rotating the same way.

**Making the motor stronger** follows from $F = BIl$: increase the **current**, use a **stronger magnetic field**, or use **more turns** on the coil so more length of wire sits in the field.

**Loudspeakers and headphones use the motor effect to convert variations in current in electrical circuits to the pressure variations in sound waves.**

**How a moving-coil loudspeaker works.** A coil is attached to a cone and sits in the field of a permanent magnet. An **alternating current** through the coil produces a force by the motor effect — and because the current **keeps reversing**, so does the force. The coil therefore **vibrates back and forth**, the cone moves with it, and the cone pushes on the air to create the **pressure variations** we hear as sound.

**The frequency of the sound matches the frequency of the current**, and a larger current gives a larger movement and therefore a louder sound.

steps.title: The generator effect
steps.body:
**If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor.** **If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced.** This is called the **generator effect**.

**Note the two ways to get it**: **move the conductor**, or **change the field**. Either will do, and what matters is that something is **changing**. Hold a wire still in a steady field and nothing at all is induced.

**The pd is induced whether or not there is a circuit.** A **current** only flows if the circuit is **complete** — a distinction worth making precisely.

**What affects the size** of the induced pd or current: the **speed** of the movement, the **strength** of the magnetic field, and the **number of turns** on the coil. Faster, stronger, more turns — all give more.

**What affects the direction**: the **direction of motion** and the **direction of the field**. Reverse either one and the induced pd reverses; reverse both and it is unchanged.

**An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change**, whether that change is the movement of the conductor or the change in the magnetic field. This is why a generator becomes **harder to turn** when it is supplying more current — you are working against the field the induced current creates.

**Uses.** **The generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.**

**Microphones use the generator effect** to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current — the exact reverse of a loudspeaker. Sound waves move a diaphragm, the diaphragm moves a **coil** near a magnet, and the movement **induces** a current that varies with the sound.

An alternator
A loudspeaker
An electric motor

steps.title: Transformers
steps.body:
**A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.** **Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.** Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents is **not required**.

**How it works.** An **alternating** current in the primary coil produces a **continually changing** magnetic field in the iron core. That changing field passes through the secondary coil and **induces** an alternating pd in it — the generator effect.

**This is why transformers need ac.** A steady dc current would give a **steady** field, which changes nothing and induces **nothing**.

steps.title: Why the grid uses high potential differences
steps.body:
**In a step-up transformer $V_s > V_p$; in a step-down transformer $V_s < V_p$.** The National Grid uses both, and the reason connects directly to the power equations.

**If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input** — which is what $V_s \times I_s = V_p \times I_p$ says.

**The consequence is the important part.** If the transformer steps the **pd up**, the **current must come down** by the same factor, because the power is unchanged. In the worked example the pd rose 5× and the current fell 5×.

**Why that matters for transmission.** Power wasted as heat in the transmission cables is given by $P = I^2R$. Because the current is **squared**, reducing the current has a very large effect: cut the current to a fifth and the power wasted falls to a **twenty-fifth**.

**So the grid steps the potential difference up** — to hundreds of thousands of volts — **before transmitting over long distances**. The current in the cables is then small, and very little energy is wasted heating them.

**It is stepped down again** near where it is used, because hundreds of thousands of volts would be far too dangerous to deliver to a house.

**Note what is not the reason.** The high pd does not make the electricity "travel faster" or "push harder". The entire benefit is the **reduction in current**, and therefore in $I^2R$ heating in the cables.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Know which equations are given.** $F = BIl$ and both **transformer** equations are **on the AQA physics equation sheet** — you apply them. $V = IR$, $P = VI$ and $P = I^2R$ are **not** — they must be recalled. Time spent memorising the wrong list is wasted twice over.

**Left hand for motors.** **F**ield, se**C**ond finger for current, thu**M**b for motion, all at **right angles**. Use it only for the **motor** effect.

**Explain a motor by opposite forces.** The two sides of the coil carry current in **opposite directions**, so the forces on them are opposite — one up, one down — and that pair of forces turns the coil. Then say what the **commutator** does: reverses the current every **half turn**, so the rotation continues instead of reversing.

**Be precise about the generator effect.** A **potential difference** is induced whenever there is **relative movement or a changing field**; a **current** flows only if the circuit is **complete**. Saying "a current is induced" without that condition is imprecise.

**Mention the opposition.** The **induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change**. This is why a generator gets harder to turn as more current is drawn — a point that separates a strong answer from a description.

**Explain why a transformer needs ac.** The secondary pd is induced by a **changing** magnetic field. A steady dc gives a **steady** field, so **nothing is induced**. This single fact explains both why transformers need ac and why the grid is ac at all.

**Get the National Grid argument exactly right.** Power is conserved, so stepping the **pd up** steps the **current down**. Wasted power is $P = I^2R$, and because current is **squared**, a five-fold reduction in current cuts the waste **twenty-five fold**. The benefit is entirely about **reducing the current** — not about the electricity moving faster or pushing harder.

**Do the transformer power calculation through the power.** Find $V_p I_p$ first, then divide by $V_s$. Trying to juggle the ratios directly is where errors creep in.

**Know what is excluded**: laminations and eddy currents in the transformer core are **not required**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **current in a wire produces a magnetic field** around it.
- Its strength depends on the **current** and the **distance** from the wire.
- A **solenoid** strengthens the field; it is **strong and uniform inside**.
- Outside, a solenoid's field is **shaped like a bar magnet's**.
- An **electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core**.
- The **motor effect**: a current-carrying conductor in a field and the magnet **exert a force on each other**.
- **Fleming's left hand**: **F**ield, se**C**ond finger current, thu**M**b motion.
- **$F = BIl$** — given on the equation sheet; B in **tesla**.
- A **motor** turns because opposite sides feel **opposite forces**.
- A **split-ring commutator** reverses the current every **half turn**.
- **Loudspeakers** use the **motor effect**; **microphones** use the **generator effect**.
- **Generator effect**: movement or a **changing field** induces a **pd**; current needs a complete circuit.
- The induced current's field **opposes the original change**.
- **Alternator → ac**; **dynamo → dc**.
- A **transformer needs ac**, because only a **changing** field induces a pd.
- **Step-up** raises pd and **lowers current**, so **$I^2R$** losses fall steeply.

questions.prompt: Explain how an electric motor works, including why the coil rotates and what keeps it rotating, and state how the motor could be made more powerful.
questions.solution:
An electric motor works by the **motor effect**: when a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, **the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other**.

The direction of that force is given by **Fleming's left-hand rule**. Holding the thumb, first finger and second finger of the **left** hand at right angles, the **first finger** points along the **field** (north to south), the **second finger** along the **current**, and the **thumb** gives the **motion** — the direction of the force on the conductor.

**Why the coil rotates.** A motor uses a **coil** of wire in a magnetic field, and the key point is that the coil has two sides carrying current in **opposite directions** — on one side the current flows away from you and on the other it flows back.

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule to each side separately, the **field is the same** for both but the **current is reversed**, so the **forces are in opposite directions**: one side is pushed **up** and the other **down**. A pair of opposite forces acting on opposite sides of the axle produces a **turning effect**, and the coil rotates.

**What keeps it rotating.** There is a problem once the coil passes the vertical position: the side that was being pushed up is now on the other side of the axle, so the same force would begin turning the coil **back**. The motor would oscillate rather than rotate.

A **split-ring commutator** solves this. It **reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn**, at exactly the moment the coil passes the vertical. Because the current reverses, the **forces reverse** too — so the side now on the left is always pushed the same way, and the coil continues turning in **one direction** instead of reversing.

**Making the motor more powerful** follows directly from the equation for the force, $F = BIl$, which is given on the equation sheet:

- **Increase the current** ($I$), which increases the force proportionally.
- **Use a stronger magnetic field** ($B$), by using a stronger permanent magnet or an electromagnet with a larger current.
- **Add more turns to the coil**, which effectively increases the length of wire ($l$) sitting in the field, so the total force and turning effect increase.

An iron core inside the coil would also increase the field strength, since iron is easily magnetised.

questions.prompt: Explain how a transformer works, why it requires an alternating current, and why the National Grid transmits electricity at a very high potential difference.
questions.solution:
**A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.** **Iron is used because it is easily magnetised**, so it carries the magnetic field efficiently from one coil to the other.

**How it works.** An **alternating** current in the primary coil produces a magnetic field in the iron core. Because the current is alternating, that field is **continually changing** — growing, collapsing and reversing. The changing field passes through the **secondary** coil, and by the **generator effect** a **potential difference is induced** across it.

The ratio of the potential differences depends on the ratio of the numbers of turns:

$$\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}$$

So a secondary with **more** turns gives a higher pd — a **step-up** transformer, where $V_s > V_p$ — and one with **fewer** turns gives a **step-down** transformer.

**Why alternating current is essential.** The secondary pd is induced only by a **changing** magnetic field. A steady **direct** current would produce a **steady, unchanging** field in the core, and a field that does not change induces **nothing at all**.

This is worth stating carefully: the output is not merely weaker with dc — there is **no output**. It is also the underlying reason the National Grid distributes ac rather than dc, since transformers are what make efficient transmission possible.

**Why the grid uses a very high potential difference.** If a transformer is 100% efficient, the **electrical power output equals the electrical power input**:

$$V_s \times I_s = V_p \times I_p$$

Because the **power is fixed**, stepping the **potential difference up** necessarily steps the **current down** by the same factor. Raising the pd five times divides the current by five.

That matters because of what is lost in the transmission cables. The cables have resistance, and the power wasted heating them is:

$$P = I^2 R$$

The current is **squared**, so reducing it has a disproportionately large effect. Cutting the current to a **fifth** reduces the wasted power to a **twenty-fifth**. Over hundreds of kilometres of cable, that is the difference between a practical grid and one that loses most of its energy before arriving.

So the sequence is: **step-up** transformers at the power station raise the pd to hundreds of thousands of volts, the electricity is transmitted at a **very small current** with minimal heating loss, and **step-down** transformers near homes and factories bring the pd back to a safe level for use.

It is worth correcting a common misconception: the high potential difference does **not** make the electricity travel faster or "push harder". The entire benefit is the **reduction in current**, and therefore in $I^2R$ heating.

examTechnique.body:
**$F = BIl$ and the transformer equations are given** on the equation sheet; $V = IR$ and the power equations are **not**. Use **Fleming's left hand** for the **motor** effect only.

Explain a motor by **opposite forces on opposite sides** plus the **commutator**. For the grid: power is conserved, so **pd up means current down**, and $P = I^2R$ makes that a large saving.
examinerErrors: Trying to recall F = BIl, which is given on the equation sheet.
Using the left-hand rule for the generator effect.
Saying a motor spins without explaining the opposite forces.
Saying a current is induced without requiring a complete circuit.
Claiming a transformer works weakly on dc rather than not at all.
Explaining the grid as high voltage "pushing harder".
Writing about eddy currents, which are not required.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer knows **which equations are given** and spends its memorising elsewhere. It explains a motor through **opposite currents giving opposite forces**, and names the **commutator**'s job precisely — reversing the current every **half turn**. On the generator effect it distinguishes the induced **pd** from the **current** that needs a complete circuit, and mentions that the induced field **opposes the original change**, which is why a generator is harder to turn under load. It states that a transformer on dc induces **nothing at all**, and it gets the grid argument exactly right: **power is conserved**, so higher pd means **lower current**, and since waste goes as $I^2R$, a five-fold cut in current is a **twenty-five-fold** cut in loss.
